God's justice, power and goodness (verses 1–8)

About a hundred years before Nahum, the people of Nineveh had repented when Jonah preached to them.

Their city was spared, but afterward they became even more wicked than before.

Nineveh did not truly know the God with whom it was contending.

Nahum therefore announced what kind of God he is.

Everyone should receive these words with faith.

They are terrifying to wicked people but comforting to believers.

Let sinners read them and tremble; let faithful people read them and rejoice.

The Lord's anger against sin is set beside his goodness toward his people.

They may be little known or respected in the world, but the Lord knows those who belong to him.

The Bible's portrait of Jehovah does not fit the notions of proud people who imagine they can decide what God must be like.

The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ is slow to anger and ready to forgive.

Yet he will not declare the unrepentant wicked innocent.

Trouble and anguish await everyone who continues doing evil.

Who pays proper attention to the power of his anger?

Assyria's destruction and the good news of peace (verses 9–15)

The powers of evil devise many plans against the Lord and his kingdom on earth.

All such plots will finally fail.

Some sinners are brought to judgment quickly.

One way or another, God will put an end to all his enemies.

People may feel calm and secure, without the least fear of disaster.

Yet they can be cut down like grass or grain when the destroying messenger passes through.

Through the downfall of Assyria, the Lord intended to bring great deliverance to his own people.

Those who disgrace themselves through conspicuous wrongdoing may be brought to public disgrace through judgment.

The news of deliverance would be welcomed with great joy.

Scripture also applies these words to the great redemption accomplished by Jesus Christ and to the lasting good news of the gospel (Romans 10:15).

Christ's ministers are messengers announcing the peace made available through him.

How welcome this message is to those who recognize the misery and danger brought upon them by sin!

Promises made to God during times of trouble should be fulfilled afterward.

Let us be thankful for his appointed ordinances and gladly take part in them.

And let us look forward with cheerful hope to a world where the wicked cannot enter and where sin and temptation will no longer be known.
classic_reading:
[Nah.1.1-Nah.1.8]
Nahum
This prophet denounces the certain and approaching destruction of the Assyrian empire, particularly of Nineveh, which is described very minutely. Together with this is consolation for his countrymen, encouraging them to trust in God.
Chapter 1
Chapter Outline
The justice and power of the Lord. | (1-8) |
The overthrow of the Assyrians. | (9-15) |
Verses 1-8
About a hundred years before, at Jonah's preaching, the Ninevites repented, and were spared, yet, soon after, they became worse than ever. Nineveh knows not that God who contends with her, but is told what a God he is. It is good for all to mix faith with what is here said concerning Him, which speaks great terror to the wicked, and comfort to believers. Let each take his portion from it: let sinners read it and tremble; and let saints read it and triumph. The anger of the Lord is contrasted with his goodness to his people. Perhaps they are obscure and little regarded in the world, but the Lord knows them. The Scripture character of Jehovah agrees not with the views of proud reasoners. The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ is slow to wrath and ready to forgive, but he will by no means acquit the wicked; and there is tribulation and anguish for every soul that doeth evil: but who duly regards the power of his wrath?
[Nah.1.9-Nah.1.15]
Verses 9-15
There is a great deal plotted against the Lord by the gates of hell, and against his kingdom in the world; but it will prove in vain. With some sinners God makes quick despatch; and one way or other, he will make an utter end of all his enemies. Though they are quiet, and many very secure, and not in fear, they shall be cut down as grass and corn, when the destroying angel passes through. God would hereby work great deliverance for his own people. But those who make themselves vile by scandalous sins, God will make vile by shameful punishments. The tidings of this great deliverance shall be welcomed with abundant joy. These words are applied to the great redemption wrought out by our Lord Jesus and the everlasting gospel, [Rom.10.15] Ro 10:15. Christ's ministers are messengers of good tidings, that preach peace by Jesus Christ. How welcome to those who see their misery and danger by sin! And the promise they made in the day of trouble must be made good. Let us be thankful for God's ordinances, and gladly attend them. Let us look forward with cheerful hope to a world where the wicked never can enter, and sin and temptation will no more be known.

Nineveh's destruction is foretold (verses 1–10)

Nineveh would not be able to turn away the judgment approaching it.

Neither human advice nor military strength can prevail against the Lord.

God looks upon proud and powerful cities and brings them low.

Nahum described in detail the terrifying appearance of the attacking army and the fear it would produce.

The Assyrian empire is pictured as a queen about to be led away captive to Babylon.

When a guilty conscience is awakened in a day of trouble, the mind may be filled with terror.

What help can stored wealth and public glory offer in such a moment, or when the day of divine wrath arrives?

Yet how many people sacrifice their souls to obtain those very things!

Assyria's cruelty brings judgment (verses 11–13)

The Assyrian kings had long terrorized their neighbors through their cruelty.

Now the Lord would break their power.

Some people excuse robbery and deceit by saying they have families to provide for.

But possessions gained through such wrongdoing will not bring lasting good to them or their households.

Those who fear the Lord and earn their living honestly may depend upon his care for themselves and those who belong to them.

God may justly remove children or the comfort parents expected to receive from them when the parents have used sinful methods to enrich the family.

People who have insulted God with their speech may find that their voices are no longer heard.

Therefore, rather than trusting in dishonest gain or worldly power, let us approach God's throne of mercy.

Through our Lord Jesus Christ we may have peace with God and know that he is for us.

Then we can trust that all things will work together for our everlasting good.

Nineveh's destruction foretold. | (1-10) |
The true cause, their sinning against God, and his appearing against them. | (11-13) |
Verses 1-10
Nineveh shall not put aside this judgment; there is no counsel or strength against the Lord. God looks upon proud cities, and brings them down. Particular account is given of the terrors wherein the invading enemy shall appear against Nineveh. The empire of Assyria is represented as a queen, about to be led captive to Babylon. Guilt in the conscience fills men with terror in an evil day; and what will treasures or glory do for us in times of distress, or in the day of wrath? Yet for such things how many lose their souls!
[Nah.2.11-Nah.2.13]
Verses 11-13
The kings of Assyria had long been terrible and cruel to their neighbours, but the Lord would destroy their power. Many plead as an excuse for rapine and fraud, that they have families to provide for; but what is thus obtained will never do them any good. Those that fear the Lord, and get honestly what they have, shall not want for themselves and theirs. It is just with God to deprive those of children, or of comfort in them, who take sinful courses to enrich them. Those are not worthy to be heard again, that have spoken reproachfully of God. Let us then come to God upon his mercy-seat, that having peace with him through our Lord Jesus Christ, we may know that he is for us, and that all things shall work together for our everlasting good.

Nineveh's sins and judgment (verses 1–7)

When proud sinners are brought down, others should learn not to become proud themselves.

The destruction of this great city warns individual people who accumulate wealth through deception and oppression.

By mistreating others, they create enemies for themselves.

If the Lord decides to punish them in this life, they may find no one willing to pity them.

Everyone who seeks personal prosperity, safety and peace should act not only honestly and honorably, but also with kindness toward all.

Nineveh's complete downfall (verses 8–19)

Even the strongest fortresses cannot protect people from God's judgments.

When he determines that they must fall, they will be unable to defend themselves.

The Chaldeans and Medes would consume the land like swarms of destructive insects.

Henry also understands the multitude of hired soldiers to be among the forces that would consume Assyria itself.

He suggests that the term translated “merchants” in this passage may refer to those troops.

Those who have done evil to their neighbors will eventually experience the consequences.

Nineveh, along with many other cities, kingdoms and empires, has been ruined.

Their histories ought to warn us.

Are we any better?

Only the presence of true believers among a people provides a stronger defense than favorable geography or military strength.

When the Lord sets himself against a nation, everything it trusts in will either fail or become a disadvantage.

But he continues to show goodness to Israel.

The Lord himself is an unconquerable stronghold for every believer in trouble.

No enemy can storm or capture that refuge.

He knows those who trust in him.

[Nah.3.1-Nah.3.7]
Chapter 3
Chapter Outline
The sins and judgments of Nineveh. | (1-7) |
Its utter destruction. | (8-19) |
Verses 1-7
When proud sinners are brought down, others should learn not to lift themselves up. The fall of this great city should be a lesson to private persons, who increase wealth by fraud and oppression. They are preparing enemies for themselves; and if the Lord sees good to punish them in this world, they will have none to pity them. Every man who seeks his own prosperity, safety, and peace, should not only act in an upright, honourable manner, but with kindness to all.
[Nah.3.8-Nah.3.19]
Verses 8-19
Strong-holds, even the strongest, are no defence against the judgments of God. They shall be unable to do any thing for themselves. The Chaldeans and Medes would devour the land like canker-worms. The Assyrians also would be eaten up by their own numerous hired troops, which seem to be meant by the word rendered "merchants." Those that have done evil to their neighbours, will find it come home to them. Nineveh, and many other cities, states, and empires, have been ruined, and should be a warning to us. Are we better, except as there are some true Christians amongst us, who are a greater security, and a stronger defence, than all the advantages of situation or strength? When the Lord shows himself against a people, every thing they trust in must fail, or prove a disadvantage; but he continues good to Israel. He is a strong-hold for every believer in time of trouble, that cannot be stormed or taken; and he knoweth those that trust in Him.
